State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
Axis Bank Credit Card Section ... vs R Santhanam S/O. J Ramakrishnan on 29 September, 2026
1

 IN THE TAMILNADU STATE CONSUMER DISPUTES
 REDRESSAL COMMISSION, CHENNAI.

 Present: Hon'ble THIRU JUSTICE R. SUBBIAH: PRESIDENT

 F.A. No.268 of 2026
[Against the order passed in C.C. No.273 of 2025 dated 28.10.2025 on
 the file of the D.C.D.R.C., Chennai (South)]

 Tuesday, the 29th day of September 2026

Axis Bank Credit Card Section
Mr.Abhinav Chaudry
Managing Director
M/s. Axis Bank Ltd.
Corporate Office
Bombay Dyeing Mills Compound
Pandurang Budhkar Marg
Worli, Mumbai- 400 025. .. Appellant/
 Opposite Party

 - Vs -

R. Santhanam
S/o. J.Ramakrishnan
B1D, Regal Palm Garden
383 Velachery Tambaram Road
Near A2B, Chennai-600 042. .. Respondent/
 Complainant

Counsel for the Appellant/
 Opposite Party : M/s. C. Prasanna Venkatesh

Respondent /Complainant : Party - in - person

 This appeal came up for final hearing on 02.09.2026, and on
hearing the arguments of the counsel for the appellant and the
 2

respondent-in-person and on perusing the material records, this
Commission made the following

 ORDER
R.SUBBIAH J., PRESIDENT

 This appeal has been filed as against the order dated

28.10.2025, passed in C.C. No.273 of 2025 by the District Consumer

Disputes Redressal Forum, Chennai (South), allowing the complaint

filed by the respondent herein.
2. The Appellant is the opposite party and the Respondent

is the complainant. For the sake of convenience, the parties will be

referred as per their ranking before the District Commission.
3. The case of the complainant as given in the

complaint filed before the District Commission is as follows:-
The complainant is a senior citizen, aged more than 79

years, undergoing treatment for Parkinson's disease. He is a customer

of the opposite party/Axis Bank for over 16 years. On 15.12.2024,

when the complainant was at home undergoing GAIT exercises for

Parkinson's disease, he heard the sound of SMS alerts in his mobile

phone. It showed three SMS messages totalling approximately

Rs.71,000/- transferred to a beneficiary named "SAMAST TEC." The
3
complainant was shocked with the messages because he had not

initiated or approved any such transaction. He immediately called the

opposite party/Axis Bank toll-free number to report the fraud and

asked them to freeze his card. He sent a WhatsApp message to the

Velachery Branch Manager Mr. Rajesh, and also spoke to him directly.

Thereafter, he reported the crime to the Cyber Crime helpline and also

filed an online cyber crime complaint and received acknowledgement.

That apart, on 03.01.2025, the complainant went to Velachery Police

Station Crime Branch and filed a complaint, for which CSR No.10/2025

was assigned. On the same day, around 6.00 pm, the complainant

called the Axis Bank toll-free number again. One Mr.Marian, an

Executive of the opposite party informed the complainant that the

amounts debited are still with the bank and has not been released to

the beneficiary. He also assured the complainant that the bank would

call or message him to check, prior to releasing the funds of the said

transactions. On 16.12.2024, the complainant sent an email to Axis

Bank's Credit Cards division, with a copy marked to Mr. Amitabh

Chaudhry, the Managing Director of Axis Bank, detailing the fraud.

But, the complainant did not receive any messages or calls on the 15th

or 16th December 2024 to check with him regarding the transactions,

prior to releasing of the said amounts. On 19.12.2024, the
4
complainant sent a complaint through email to the
[email protected]
along with the details of the transactions

made to "SAMAST TEC" fraudulently. Since there was no response for

the earlier mails from the opposite party Bank, the complainant sent a

reminder on 22.12.2024 to the Axis Bank customer care (credit cards

division),
[email protected]
and Mr. Amitabh

Chaudhry. Though the complainant received the usual monthly credit

card statement on 24.12.2024, he could not open despite trying

various methods provided by the bank. Hence, he asked the Bank to

send a printed copy of his credit card statement so that he could

review the same and check whether any other recent fraudulent or

criminal transactions had taken place. Yet another reminder was sent

on 27.12.2024 to the
[email protected]
and

Mr.Amitabh Chaudhry. A reminder requesting for the printed copy of

the statement was also sent via email to
[email protected]
Inspite of

repeated reminders, there was no response from the opposite party.

Hence, the complainant went in person to the Velachery branch of the

opposite party Bank to collect the statement. The complainant was

shocked to notice from the statement that while the transactions were

shown as being initiated on 15.12.2024, their postings were on

16.12.2024, which means that the amounts were transferred only as
5
stated by the Executive of the opposite party Bank that the Bank

would check with him before proceeding with the said transaction.
Whileso, the opposite party Bank had issued a legal notice dated

12.05.2025 to the complainant directing him to clear the outstanding

dues of Rs.1,21,197/-, which was suitably replied by the complainant

vide notice dated 22.05.2025 sent through his counsel. Thus, alleging

deficiency of service on the part of the opposite party, the complainant

has filed the present complaint to direct the opposite party,

 a. To withdraw their claim of Rs.71,000/- along with interest
 and penalty against the credit card
 No.5546370228685373; and

 b. to pay a sum of Rs.4,00,000/- as compensation for the
 mental anguish undergone by the complainant.
4. Resisting the case of the complainant, the opposite

party has filed a written version stating that the complaint is not

maintainable either in law or on facts. The complainant seeks to

saddle the Bank with liability for certain disputed transactions which

were carried out through valid two-factor authentication using card

details and OTPs sent to the registered mobile number. Such

transactions are conclusively established as customer-induced and

hence there is no deficiency of service on the part of the opposite
6
party. The complainant Mr.Ramakrishnan Santhanam, raised a

grievance with respect to his Axis Bank Credit Card bearing number

5546370228685373 and Savings Account No. 014010100674456. The

complaint was assigned with SR No.250128588063 and Complaint No.

SAK00002917838. The disputed transactions, amounting to

Rs.70,648/- pertain to three on-line purchases made on 15.12.2024 at

merchant "Cashfree -Samast Techno, Gurgaon". The disputed

transaction amounts are, (i) Rs.24,968.20; (ii) Rs.21,372.60; and (iii)

Rs.24,638.94 and all were executed on 15.12.2024. Each of these

transactions was processed on the basis of the card number, CVV and

One-Time Password (OTP) that was delivered to the registered mobile

number 9940144690 of the Complainant. The delivery of OTP and

successful completion of 2FA establishes that the transactions were

duly authorized through secured channels known only to the

cardholder. The opposite party Bank immediately conducted a

detailed investigation vide Case ID 175357. The E-commerce

Investigation Report concluded that no unauthorized demographic

change such as mobile number or email address modification was

observed. It was found that the OTPs were delivered to the

complainant's registered number and were successfully used for the

transactions. The transactions were therefore secured and completed
7
using the credentials known only to the complainant, and no system or

security lapse had occurred at the Bank's end. It was also found in the

said investigation that the complainant had been using his credit card

for e-commerce transactions including Airtel, thereby showing

familiarity with online card usage. It was also noted that transaction

monitoring alerts were not triggered since the transactions did not

breach the system's rule thresholds, which are scientifically set on the

basis of customer profile, spending patterns and merchant categories.

Consequently, customer liability was crystallized for the entire amount

of Rs.70,648/-. Subsequently, the complainant reported another

disputed Internet Banking transaction of Rs.22,805.90 on 30.12.2024.

The investigation under Case ID NO.186773 for the said dispute

revealed that the complainant had received a WhatsApp call from a

fraudster impersonating an Axis Bank employee. During the call, the

complainant was induced to share the details of his Axis Bank and

ICICI Bank accounts, leading to fraudulent IMPS debits. The

investigation further revealed that the complainant himself has reset

his Internet Banking password using the "forgot password" link,

validated by OTP and email link sent to his registered credentials. The

beneficiary was added and transaction executed only upon entry of

OTP received on the complainant's registered mobile number. The
8
Internet Banking Investigation further concluded that there were no

unauthorized demographic changes or suspicious access from Bank

staff, and that the liability devolved entirely upon the complainant due

to compromise of confidential credentials through a vishing call. The

matter was therefore categorized as "Fraud," with customer liability of

Rs.22,805.90. In parallel, the CRM Service Request records reflect

that the complaints were escalated to the Internal Ombudsman for

review. The Internal Ombudsman categorically noted that the disputed

transactions were customer-induced, secured electronic transactions,

carried out through OTP sent to the registered mobile. It was

concluded that such transactions cannot be carried out without the

cardholder sharing confidential details with a third party, knowingly or

unknowingly. The Ombudsman therefore concurred with the Bank's

decision that no liability devolves on the Bank. The opposite party

reiterates that as per the cardholder terms and conditions, the

complainant is solely responsible for safeguarding his confidential

credentials namely, card number, CVV, PIN, OTP, and passwords. Any

compromise of such information at the customer's end absolves the

Bank from liability. The Bank's role is limited to processing instructions

validated through secured two-factor authentication, which in the

present case was strictly complied with. The complainant has alleged
9
deficiency of service and failure of security, which is specifically

denied. The Bank's systems were robust, OTPs were delivered

successfully and SMS alerts were sent on the day of transactions. The

security mechanisms had worked as intended. The unfortunate loss

suffered by the complainant arose solely from compromise of

confidential credentials, which are within the control of the

complainant and not the opposite party. The Reserve Bank of India

guidelines on electronic transactions clearly stipulate that where loss

occurs due to the negligence of the customer in sharing payment

credentials, the liability is that of the customer. Only in cases where

the deficiency is attributable to the Bank, the opposite party can be

held liable. The present case falls squarely within the category of

customer liability, as has been confirmed by the Bank's investigation,

the CRM resolution team and the Internal Ombudsman. The opposite

party has, in good faith, advised the complainant to pursue the matter

with law enforcement authorities by lodging a police complaint so that

the culprits may be identified and proceeded against. The opposite

party has also confirmed that it shall extend full cooperation to the

police authorities in their investigation. However, the liability for

repayment of the disputed amounts continues to rest on the

complainant and the opposite party cannot be compelled to reimburse
10
the said amount, which is the outcome of customer's negligence.

Therefore, the complaint is misconceived, vexatious, and liable to be

dismissed with exemplary costs, as it seeks to hold the opposite party

Bank liable for the actions and omissions attributed solely by the

complainant. Thus, there is no deficiency in service or unfair trade

practice on the part of the Bank. Further, the complainant has not

produced any cogent material to show that the Bank's systems were

faulty or that the transactions were processed without his

authorization. On the contrary, the evidence in the form of OTP logs,

SMS delivery records and investigation reports clearly establish that all

security layers were intact and successfully completed. The allegation

of unauthorized debit is therefore unfounded. The complainant has

failed to discharge his contractual duty of maintaining the secrecy of

his credentials. The terms and conditions governing the issuance and

usage of credit cards, as duly accepted by the complainant at the time

of availing the facility, impose an obligation on the cardholder to

ensure confidentiality of all verification information. The breach of such

obligation disentitles the complainant from claiming restitution from

the Bank. The claim for refund of the disputed amounts is to unjust

enrichment, as the transactions in question were executed with valid

authentication and the Bank has neither gained nor benefitted from
11
the same. The funds have been transferred to third-party merchants

or beneficiaries based on the instructions validated through the

customer's credentials, and the Bank has no legal duty to indemnify

losses occasioned by the customer's negligence. The complainant's

subsequent allegation of vishing fraud regarding Internet Banking only

reinforces the security compromise occurred at his end. Having once

been defrauded, the complainant was expected to exercise heightened

vigilance. Instead, by voluntarily disclosing the account details to an

unknown caller, he had further compromised his banking security. The

Bank cannot be penalized for such acts of the complainant. The

opposite party reiterates that it has acted in utmost good faith by

providing the complainant with detailed investigation reports, Internal

Ombudsman review, and also advised to approach the police

authorities. The Bank had also ensured that all his banking channels

were secured by blocking the compromised card. Therefore, absolutely

there is no deficiency of service or unfair trade practice on the part of

the opposite party Bank and hence sought for dismissal of the

complaint.
12
5. In order to prove the case, on the side of the

complainant, along with proof affidavit 14 documents were filed, which

were marked as Exhibits A1 to A14. On the side of the opposite party,

proof affidavit and 5 documents were filed and the same were marked

as Ex.B1 to B5.
6. The District Commission had observed that the

complainant had immediately reported the fraudulent transactions to

the Bank's toll free number on the same day and also through emails.

Irrespective of the liabilities of the parties, under the zero liability

policy of the RBI, banks are required to compensate the customer for

fraudulent transactions made without their authorization. Eventhough

the transactions had been fraudulent, the opposite party had issued a

legal notice to the complainant demanding repayment of the overdue

amount on the credit card. Such a demand made by the opposite

party is not acceptable because the complainant had not used a single

rupee for his own benefit. Ex.A4, A5, B1 and B2 clearly shows that the

transactions were fraudulent. On the same day, the complainant had

sent emails and WhatsApp messages reporting the fraudulent

transactions. Even after receiving these messages, the disputed
13
amount had been transferred on 15.12.2024 from the opposite party

Bank. The complainant had sent several emails to the opposite party

seeking a printed copy of the credit card statement. However, the

opposite party had not provided the same. Moreover, the opposite

party themselves had investigated and found the transaction made on

15.12.2024 using the complainant's credit card is fraudulent. Though

the opposite party had admitted that the transactions were fraudulent,

they have sent a legal notice to the complainant demanding the credit

card payment, as overdue. The said act of negligence and deficiency

in service on the part of the opposite party had caused severe mental

agony to the complainant, who is a senior citizen, aged about 80

years. Hence the District Commission allowed the complaint and

directed the opposite party not to claim the sum of Rs.71,000/- and

the associated interest and penalty from the complainant; and to pay

a sum of Rs.2,00,000/- as compensation for the loss incurred and the

mental agony suffered by the complainant along with a sum of

Rs.15,000/- towards the cost of the complaint. Aggrieved over the

said order, the present appeal has been filed by the opposite party.
14
7. It is the submission of the learned counsel for the

appellant/opposite party that the impugned order proceeds upon a

fundamental misreading of the record and upon a conflation of two

entirely distinct and unconnected incidents. The relief granted and the

reasoning given are unsupported by any finding of deficiency in service

on the part of the appellant/opposite party Bank, and are, in fact,

contradicted by the very documents that the District Commission has

relied upon. The impugned order therefore suffers from non-

application of mind, mis-appreciation of evidence and material

irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction. It is the case of the

appellant/opposite party that the respondent/complainant was the

holder of the credit card No.5546370228685373 (Indian Oil Axis Bank

Premium Credit Card) issued by the appellant/opposite party Bank and

his registered mobile number (RMN) with the Bank was 91-

9940144690. On 15.12.2024, three e-commerce transactions were

carried out on the said credit card in favour of the online merchant

'Cashfree SAMAST TECHNO', namely Rs.24,638.94, Rs.21,372.60 and

Rs.24,968.20, aggregating to approximately Rs.71,000/-. Each of the

three transactions was completed using the respondent/complainant's

complete confidential card credentials, namely, the 16-digit card

number, the expiry date and the CVV number -- in conjunction with
15
One-Time Passwords (OTPs) that were generated by the Bank and

delivered to the respondent/complainant's registered mobile number.

The OTP logs and SMS delivery logs are produced as Ex.B4 to establish

that OTPs were transmitted to the RMN No.91-9940144690 for the

transaction of Rs.24,638.94 at 11:05:38 hrs, for the transaction of

Rs.21,372.60 at 11:07:41 hrs and for the transaction of Rs.24,968.20

at 11:09:33 hrs., on 15.12.2024. Based on the report of the

respondent/ complainant that the said transactions as fraudulent,

immediately the appellant/ opposite party Bank blocked the credit card

on 15.12.2024 at 11:41:56 hrs and conducted a detailed investigation

through its E-commerce Transaction Investigation cell (Incident Id

No.175357), the report marked as Ex.B1, which conclusively found

that the transactions were two-factor authenticated secured

transactions completed using the customer's complete credentials and

transaction OTPs, which are known only to the customer, that no alert

was warranted as the transactions were within the assigned

parameters and that the customer had used the very same card for e-

commerce transactions in the past. The investigation concluded that

there was no deficiency, security lapse or system breach on the part of

the Bank, and that no liability devolves on the Bank. It is pertinent to

state that the loss complained with respect to the credit card ending
16
5373, stands on an entirely separate footing from a subsequent and

unconnected incident. By his own admission, and as borne out by his

own documents, on 30.12.2024 the respondent/complainant had

received a vishing call from a person impersonating an Axis Bank

official named 'Ravi Mishra', and was persuaded to part with his KYC

details, card details and account details, and also had enabled screen-

sharing/ install an application (APK) upon his device, following which a

further sum of Rs.22,805.90 was fraudulently transferred from his Axis

Bank savings account through an IMPS transaction and he also lost a

further sum of Rs.45,955/- from his ICICI Bank account. This incident

which happened on 30.12.2024, was separately investigated by the

Bank's Internet Banking Investigation cell (Incident Id 186773), the

report marked as Ex.B2, which was likewise concluded that since the

loss arose from the compromise of confidential credentials and OTPs at

the customer's end, no liability devolves on the Bank. The direction

impugned in the present Appeal concerns only to the credit card claim

of Rs.71,000/-; the savings account and ICICI losses happened on

30.12.2024 are neither the subject of the Bank's claim nor of the

impugned direction. The matter was escalated and independently

examined by the Bank's Internal Ombudsman, whose remarks were

recorded in the CRM Service Request records, marked as Ex.B3 and
17
the Credit Card IO Form, marked as Ex.B5. The said report expressly

concurred with the Bank's decision, holding that the disputed

transactions were customer-induced secured electronic transactions

completed through OTPs sent to the registered mobile number, that

such transactions could not have been done unless the person was in

possession of all the confidential card details known only to the

account holder, and that, in all probability, the customer had divulged

such information to a third party, knowingly or unknowingly, whereby

no liability devolves on the Bank. The District Commission had

conflated the credit card transactions of 15.12.2024 with the separate

savings account of ICICI losses on 30.12.2024; Further, the District

Commission had misapplied the concept of 'Zero Liability' to a case

squarely arising out of customer-end negligence; Although the Bank's

investigation reports, exonerates the Bank, it is misread by the District

Commission as though they fastened the liability on the Bank; It is

clear from the reports that there is no deficiency in service, security

lapse or system breach on the part of the Bank. It is a settled position

that successful use of an OTP creates a strong presumption of

authorisation by the cardholder. A credit card e-commerce transaction

of this nature cannot be completed unless the person effecting it, is

simultaneously in possession of the 16-digit card number, the expiry
18
date, the CVV and the OTP delivered to the registered mobile number.

Of these, the OTP is transmitted exclusively to the RMN, and all of

these particulars are within the sole knowledge and control of the

cardholder. Having placed on record substantial and uncontroverted

material to demonstrate that the authentication process was duly and

successfully completed, the issuing Bank cannot, in such

circumstances, be fastened with liability. The District Commission had

failed to consider that the proximate cause of the alleged loss was the

respondent/ complainant's own failure to safeguard his confidential

card credentials and OTP. Since the transactions were authenticated

using particulars known only to the respondent/complainant, the only

rational inference is that those particulars were compromised at the

respondent/complainant's end. Significantly, this inference is not

merely the Bank's assertion but it is established by the respondent/

complainant's own documents, namely, the Cyber Crime complaint

(marked as Ex.A4), his Airtel call log on 30.12.2024 (marked as

Ex.A11) and his 'Recorded Conversation with Fraudster' on 30.12.2024

(marked as Ex.A12) demonstrate, in his own words, the precise modus

operandi by which he was induced by fraudsters to divulge his KYC,

card and account details and to install a screen-sharing application,

resulting in further losses on 30.12.2024. This admitted conduct
19
establishes a clear pattern of the respondent/complainant parting with

his confidential credentials to third parties. Further, in a real time

automated payment system, once a credit card transaction is

authenticated using the correct credentials and the OTP, it stands

irrevocably authorised and cannot thereafter be unilaterally stopped,

held or reversed by the issuing Bank. The three transactions were

authenticated between 11.05 and 11.10 hours on 15.12.2024, which is

before the respondent/complainant made any report. The reference

made by the District Commission to the transactions being 'posted' on

16.12.2024 is misconceived. The posting date reflects merely the

accounting and settlement date within the card system and does not

represent a fresh authorisation or a discretionary 'release' that the

bank could have withheld. There was, in law and in fact, nothing left

to 'hold'. Further, the Bank has at no stage admitted any fraud,

negligence or deficiency of its own. The issuance of a recovery or

demand communication in respect of an outstanding sum on a duly

authenticated credit card is a standard and legitimate contractual

process, flowing from the fact that the sums were disbursed to the

merchant upon authenticated transactions and hence the same does

not constitute deficiency in service or admission of liability. Thus it is

made clear that the loss is only due to the negligence of the
20
respondent/complainant and that there is no deficiency of service on

the part of the opposite party. Therefore, the order of the District

Commission is contrary to law, opposed to the facts and evidence on

record and unsustainable and hence the appellant/ opposite party

prayed this Commission to set aside the order of the District

Commission.
8. Per contra, it is the submission of the respondent/

complainant in person that despite multiple unusual transactions

occurring within a very short span of time, including the rejection of

the fourth transaction, the appellant/opposite party Bank failed to

contact the respondent/complainant over phone or any other effective

means to verify whether the transactions were genuinely authorized by

him. Immediately upon noticing the unauthorized transactions, the

respondent/complainant acted diligently by calling the appellant/

opposite party Bank's customer care and requested to block the credit

card. Though the three e-commerce fraudulent transactions were

informed immediately, the appellant/opposite party did not take any

effort to investigate the matter by contacting the beneficiary. Since

the respondent/complainant was not furnished with the monthly credit
21
card statement he went to the Bank in person and obtained the same,

which revealed that though the disputed transactions happened on

15.12.2024, the appellant/opposite party had released the disputed

amounts only on 16.12.2024, without verifying the authenticity of the

transaction from the respondent/complainant. The respondent/

complainant had independently identified and contacted the

beneficiary of the fraudulent transaction, over phone and email and

had forwarded all such communications to the appellant/opposite party

for taking appropriate action. But, the appellant/ opposite party had

failed to take any action to recover the disputed amounts. Therefore,

there is clear deficiency of service on the part of the appellant/

opposite party and sought to dismiss the appeal.
9. Heard the submissions made by the learned counsel for

the appellant/opposite party and the respondent/complainant in-

person, in detail and I have carefully gone through the entire material

available on records.
10. When the matter was taken up for consideration, it is

seen that the way in which the complaint is drafted appears to be

obscure that facts are presented by the complainant in a jumbled
22
manner with a lot of repetitions completely bereft of cogency and the

endeavour of the complainant is to somehow fill up the pages with

some talkative and irrelevant narratives which would definitely irk

anyone tasked to go through the contents. In a disposal mechanism

involving summary procedure for delivering quick consumer justice,

the parties are implicitly required to present facts in a clear, cogent

and concise manner and to submit the arguments straight to the

points and issues, enabling the Commission to easily grasp the things

for discussion and reaching a fair and right decision, but here, the

complainant had actuated by his bad zeal to catch numerous fishes

with a single hook, made preparations in such a haste and hurry that

ultimately, for culling out the facts and collating everything in order

with cogency, this Commission is driven to unnecessarily spend its

sizeable time. Only from the arguments and submissions made on the

side of the opposite party and based on the records available, this

Commission has come to understand the actual facts about the case.
11. At any rate, as to the course of action taken by the

Bank it is seen that the respondent/ complainant reported about the

fraudulent transactions on 15.12.2024 and immediately thereupon, the

Bank had blocked the credit card, and that detailed investigations have
23
been conducted through E-commerce Transaction Investigation cell

and also by way of Internet Banking Investigation and the reports are

marked as Ex.B1 and B2. Further evidence in the form of IP logs and

SMS/OTP logs are marked as Ex.B4 to establish that there was no

security lapse or system breach. The set of technical evidence and

reports of the Bank were considered by the Internal Ombudsman to

hold that no liability devolves on the Bank and the report is marked as

Ex.B3.
On a close perusal, we find that the disputed transactions

were Card-Not-Present (CNP) transactions. Though the physical credit

card remained in the possession of the respondent/complainant, the

transactions were completed using the complete card credentials,

namely the card number, expiry date and CVV, along with transaction-

specific OTPs. The OTPs were sent to the registered mobile number

(RMN) with the credit card account, and transaction alerts were

likewise transmitted to the registered mobile number. The

investigation on the part of the bank reveals no unauthorised change

in the registered mobile number or e-mail address prior to the

disputed transactions. To cull out, what appears from the outcome of

the investigation in a wholesome manner :-
24
a) the disputed transactions were CNP transactions;
b) the physical card remained in the possession of the

 respondent/complainant;
c) the transactions were completed using the card number,

 expiry date and CVV;
d) transaction-specific OTPs were generated and successfully

 used;
e) the OTPs were sent to the registered mobile number;
f) on usage of OTPs the transactions were secured and the

 transaction messages were sent to the registered mobile

 number;
g) there was no detected unauthorised alteration of the

 registered mobile number or e-mail address prior to the

 transactions; and
h) the respondent/complainant reported the disputed

 transactions to the bank and cyber crime immediately.
Ultimately, the investigation reports under Exs.B1 and B3, both

conclude the instance as 'fraud' in nature, adding that no liability lies

on the Bank. The matter does not end with those investigations. A

vital aspect that emerges from the records is that Ex.A9, which is an
25
email subsequently sent by the respondent/complainant to the

recipient agency, states, in substance, that a fraudster had hacked his

mobile and transferred the disputed amounts to the said agency in

three transactions, requesting that the necessary action be taken. This

communication becomes significant in the chronology of events, for, it

was not the explanation initially placed by the respondent/complainant

before the appellant/opposite party Bank when the disputed

transactions were first reported. It was only subsequently about 4 to 5

months later, and after the Bank had undertaken its investigation into

the transactions, that the respondent/complainant attributed the

disputed transfers to a specific intervening event, namely, the alleged

hacking of his mobile device. The said communication, therefore,

cannot be considered divorced from the investigation already

undertaken by the Bank, nor can the subsequent course adopted by

the Bank in treating the disputed amount as recoverable from the

respondent/complainant and issuing the legal notice under Ex.A13

demanding payment be considered independently of the same

evidentiary circumstances. In other words, the investigation

undertaken by the appellant/opposite party Bank and the materials

disclosed thereby, the subsequent conduct of the respondent/

complainant in addressing the recipient agency under Ex.A9 and the
26
action of the Bank in proceeding to recover the disputed amount from

the respondent/complainant, when considered together having regard

to the findings and reasoning contained in the impugned order, bring

into focus a question which lies at the very heart of the controversy.

The question is not merely whether the disputed transactions were

unauthorised, nor can it be answered merely by noticing that the

Bank's investigation recorded successful authentication of the

transactions. What requires determination is the legal significance to

be attached to the entire evidentiary sequence and, in particular,

whether the material which is sufficient to negative a finding of Bank-

side fraud, negligence or deficiency is, by that very fact, also sufficient

to establish the respondent/complainant's liability for the disputed

transactions and thereby justify the subsequent recovery action taken

against him. It is in this backdrop and upon a cumulative

consideration of the original complaint, the course and outcome of the

Bank's investigation, the subsequent assertion contained in the SMS

the absence or otherwise of corroboration of the alleged mobile

compromise, the identifiable destination of the disputed funds, and the

consequential recovery action initiated by the appellant/opposite party

Bank, that the following question arises for determination:
27
"Whether, on the material available on

 record, the disputed transactions can legally be

 fastened upon the appellant/opposite party Bank

 as loss arising from fraud, negligence or

 deficiency attributable to it, and, if not, whether

 the very same material is nevertheless sufficient

 to affirmatively establish, in accordance with the

 governing regulatory framework and the burden

 cast upon the appellant/opposite party Bank, the

 liability of the respondent/complainant for the

 said transactions so as to sustain the

 consequential demand and recovery action

 initiated against him."
The answer to the above question necessarily requires the regulatory

scheme by way of RBI Circular DBR.No.Leg.BC.78/09.07.005/2017-18

dated 6th July 2017 governing unauthorised electronic transactions to

be applied not in the abstract, but to the precise evidentiary

circumstances disclosed by the record. The disputed transactions,

admittedly being CNP transactions, fall within the category of

remote/online payment transactions contemplated by paragraph 3(i)

of the RBI Circular. The significance of that classification lies in the fact
28
that the regulatory framework does not treat every disputed electronic

transaction as giving rise, by that circumstance alone, to an automatic

liability upon the Bank. The liability which may be cast upon the Bank,

and the circumstances in which the customer may be relieved of the

loss, are governed by the specific contingencies prescribed in the

Circular. In this regard, Paragraph 6(i) contemplates zero liability

where the unauthorised transaction is attributable to contributory

fraud, negligence or deficiency on the part of the Bank, whereas

paragraph 6(ii) concerns the situation of a third-party breach where

the deficiency lies neither with the Bank nor with the customer,

subject to the conditions stipulated therein. The distinction is material.

The mere fact that a transaction is disputed as unauthorised does not,

without more, establish either that the Bank was deficient or that a

third-party breach of the kind contemplated by paragraph 6(ii) has

occurred. The regulatory protection is thus circumstance-

dependent; it is not founded upon the mere occurrence of an

electronic transaction which the customer subsequently

disowns. Equally relevant is paragraph 12, which places upon the

Bank the burden of proving customer liability in a case of an

unauthorised electronic banking transaction. The provision assumes

significance in the present case because the enquiry cannot
29
legitimately stop upon a finding that the appellant/opposite party Bank

has not been shown to be at fault. The absence of Bank-side fraud,

negligence or deficiency may answer the first limb of the controversy;

it does not, without a further evidentiary foundation, answer the

distinct question whether the Bank had affirmatively established that

the customer is liable for the disputed transactions. The two enquiries,

though arising from the same transaction, operate upon different legal

considerations and cannot be collapsed into one.
Upon testing the Bank's investigation against that

framework, once again, it could be seen from the investigation

records/Exs.B1 and B3 that the disputed transactions were CNP

transactions; that the physical card continued to remain in the

possession of the respondent/ complainant; that the requisite OTPs

were generated and successfully used; and that no unauthorised

alteration of the registered mobile number or email address was

detected. These are positive circumstances emerging from the

transaction records and the Bank's investigation. Although they

demonstrate the manner in which the transactions were processed and

authenticated and constitute relevant material for determining whether

any act, omission, deficiency or security failure attributable to the

Bank has been established, the evidentiary value of these
30
circumstances, however, must be confined to what they actually

establish. Successful generation and use of an OTP establishes that the

authentication mechanism recorded a successful OTP event; it does

not, by itself, identify the person who caused the CNP transaction to

be initiated. Likewise, the fact that the physical card remained in the

respondent/complainant's possession is relevant, but cannot, in the

context of a card-not-present transaction, be treated as conclusive

proof of personal authorisation. Similarly, the fact that no

unauthorised alteration of the registered mobile number or email

address was detected establishes no such alteration was detected; it

does not, without more, exclude every possible form of compromise of

the device or credentials through which the transaction may have been

authenticated.
It is at this point that the email dated 05.06.2025 under

Ex.A9 assumes its proper evidentiary significance. It must be

highlighted that the said mail addressed by the respondent/

complainant to the recipient agency cannot be treated as an admission

that he authorised the disputed transactions. Nor does the mere

subsequent emergence of the allegation that his mobile had been

hacked establish that he was himself responsible for the transactions.

Its significance lies in the fact that the respondent/complainant, after
31
the Bank's investigation had been undertaken, identified a particular

intervening mechanism--namely, alleged compromise of his mobile

device--as the explanation for the transfer of the disputed amounts.

Having chosen to place that specific explanation on record, the

respondent/complainant necessarily assumed the evidentiary burden

of furnishing some material capable of lending support to that

particular explanation. But, no such independent corroboration is

shown from the material presently available. There is no demonstrated

evidence of actual compromise of the mobile device, unauthorised

access to the relevant credentials, or any other material establishing

that such compromise was the mechanism through which the three

disputed transactions were effected. The subsequent assertion

therefore remains an explanation unsupported by corroborative

evidence. Its evidentiary weakness is a circumstance which may

legitimately be taken into account while examining whether the case

falls within paragraph 7(i); but it cannot, by the same token, be

converted into affirmative proof that the respondent/complainant

himself authorised the transactions.
One more aspect is, this distinction becomes particularly

significant in view of the "identifiable destination" of the disputed

funds. The three transactions were not ones in which the destination of
32
the funds remained unknown. The amounts were transferred to an

identifiable recipient agency/SAMAST Tec, and Ex.A9 and A12 itself

brought that recipient directly into the factual narrative by informing it

that the transfers had allegedly been made by a fraudster. Once that

circumstance emerged, the recipient agency constituted a potentially

relevant evidentiary source concerning the transaction trail. It is not

suggested that the Bank was required to presume wrongdoing on the

part of the recipient agency merely because the disputed funds

reached it. Nor would the mere absence of an investigation of that

agency, by itself, establish negligence or deficiency on the part of the

Bank. The significance of the matter is narrower but nevertheless

important. Where the Bank seeks to establish, in discharge of the

burden imposed by paragraph 12, that the customer is liable for the

disputed transactions, and where an identifiable recipient forms a link

in the chain through which the disputed funds passed, material

obtained from that recipient could potentially have either corroborated

or contradicted the complainant's subsequent explanation. The records

of the appellant/opposite party Bank, however, do not disclose that

such recipient-side enquiry was undertaken. Let us make it clear, that

omission cannot be treated as proof that the recipient agency was

responsible for the transactions. No such conclusion is warranted on
33
the material before this Commission. But the point is, the evidentiary

gap thereby left cannot be filled by presuming customer liability. The

appellant/opposite party Bank cannot derive an affirmative case of

customer liability merely from the failure of the respondent/

complainant to prove his own alternative theory. If the allegation of

mobile compromise is insufficiently established to attract paragraph

7(ii), that establishes no more than that the respondent/complainant

has failed to bring his case within that particular regulatory

contingency. It does not follow, either logically or by operation of the

Circular, that the disputed transactions thereby become transactions

for which the respondent/complainant is affirmatively liable.
The same distinction answers the first limb of the

controversy. The materials on record do not establish that the disputed

transactions were attributable to contributory fraud, negligence or

deficiency on the part of the appellant/opposite party Bank. There is

no demonstrated alteration of the registered mobile number or email

address; the recorded authentication mechanism shows successful OTP

use; the physical card remained with the respondent/complainant; and

the subsequent allegation of mobile compromise remains unsupported

by independent material. On the evidence available, therefore, the

essential causal nexus between the disputed transactions and any
34
fraud, negligence, deficiency or security failure attributable to the

Bank has not been established. That conclusion, however, does not

dispose of the second limb. The very same material must then be

tested against paragraph 12. The Bank has established the

circumstances in which the transactions were processed and

authenticated. It has not, by those circumstances alone, established

the identity of the person who initiated the CNP transactions, nor has

it established any specific act of customer negligence, such as

voluntary disclosure or sharing of credentials, which would

independently furnish the basis for fastening the loss upon the

respondent/complainant. The absence of evidence establishing

Bank deficiency cannot be transposed into affirmative evidence

establishing customer liability.
It is in the above context that the reasoning of the District

Commission requires examination. The said commission appears to

have proceeded principally upon the footing that, since the

appellant/opposite party Bank's own investigation had treated the

disputed transactions as fraudulent/unauthorised, the subsequent

issuance of a legal notice demanding payment of the corresponding

overdue credit-card amount constituted negligence and deficiency in

service. In our considered opinion, that reasoning does not sufficiently
35
distinguish between the Bank's internal classification of a transaction

as fraudulent or unauthorised and an adjudicatory determination that

the appellant/opposite party Bank itself was responsible for the

resulting loss. The fact that the appellant/opposite party Bank, upon

investigation, treated the transactions as fraudulent or unauthorised

does not amount, by itself, to an admission that the fraud was

attributable to any negligence, deficiency or security failure on the part

of the Bank. The description of a transaction as fraudulent answers

one factual question concerning the nature of the transaction; it does

not, without more, determine the legal allocation of the resulting loss.

That allocation has to be made by applying the specific contingencies

contemplated by paragraphs 7(i) and 7(ii), together with the burden

imposed by paragraph 12. The District Commission was therefore

correct in taking note of the appellant/opposite party Bank's own

investigation and in treating the disputed transactions as

unauthorised/ fraudulent for the purpose of examining the complaint;

but it could not, merely from that circumstance, draw the further

conclusion that the appellant/opposite party Bank had thereby

admitted legal liability for the underlying loss. The Bank's internal

characterisation of the transactions as fraudulent does not, by itself,

constitute an admission of Bank-side fraud, negligence, deficiency or
36
security failure. Consequently, the finding that the subsequent

issuance of the legal notice, merely because it followed the

appellant/opposite party Bank's classification of the transactions as

fraudulent, constituted negligence or deficiency cannot be sustained on

that premise. The investigation undertaken by the appellant/opposite

party Bank did not amount to an admission that the loss was

attributable to Bank-side deficiency; nor does the material on record

establish such deficiency merely because the appellant/opposite party

Bank thereafter sought recovery of the outstanding amount.
But the matter cannot, for the same reason, be carried to

the opposite extreme. The appellant/opposite party Bank's failure to

establish its own liability does not dispense with the burden resting

upon it under paragraph 12 of the RBI circular. The Bank cannot

obtain an affirmative finding of customer liability merely by

demonstrating that its own systems recorded successful authentication

and that no alteration in the registered contact particulars was

detected. Those circumstances are relevant and probative; they are

not, without the missing evidentiary link, conclusive of personal

authorisation or customer negligence. The consequence for the

recovery action must therefore be examined separately. The issuance

of a demand notice for an amount asserted by a creditor to be due
37
cannot, in the abstract and merely by its issuance, be characterised as

negligence or deficiency in service. The legal character of such demand

depends upon the status of the underlying liability and the regulatory

requirements governing disputed credit-card dues. Where the

underlying transactions remain specifically disputed and the Bank has

not affirmatively established customer liability in accordance with the

governing framework, the Bank cannot treat the disputed amount as

though its liability upon the customer had already been conclusively

adjudicated merely because the Bank itself has not been shown to be

responsible for the loss. This distinction is of particular relevance to

the impugned order. The finding of the District Commission that the

legal/demand notice itself constituted deficiency merely because the

appellant/opposite party Bank had internally treated the transactions

as fraudulent cannot be sustained; at the same time, it also does not

mean that the disputed amount thereby stands affirmatively

established as a "debt payable by the appellant/opposite party to the

complainant". The question whether the appellant/opposite party Bank

may recover the disputed amount cannot be answered by simply

reversing the evidentiary burden which paragraph 12 places upon it.

Let us state the position with precision that - the evidence is

insufficient to fasten the underlying transaction loss upon the Bank
38
under paragraph 6(i), and the subsequent unsupported allegation of

mobile hacking is insufficient to establish the third-party-breach

circumstance contemplated under paragraph 6(ii); yet, the same

evidence, tested against paragraph 12, is also insufficient by

itself to affirmatively establish that the respondent/

complainant authorised the disputed transactions or is

otherwise liable for the resulting loss. These two conclusions are

not inconsistent as they arise from two separate enquiries governed by

different evidentiary requirements. The absence of a recipient-side

investigation assumes significance only in this limited context. It does

not establish appellant/opposite party deficiency; it does not establish

fraud by the recipient agency; and it does not establish the truth of

the respondent/complainant's subsequent allegation. It does, however,

demonstrate that an identifiable evidentiary avenue bearing upon the

question of customer liability was not pursued, and that the resulting

evidentiary gap cannot legitimately be filled by presumption against

the respondent/complainant when the regulatory framework expressly

places the burden of proving customer liability upon the Bank.

Therefore, the direction of the District Commission to pay a

compensation of Rs.2 lakhs must therefore be examined on the correct

footing. If the direction was founded solely upon the proposition that
39
the appellant/opposite party Bank's own classification of the

transactions as fraudulent amounted to an admission of Bank

negligence or deficiency, that reasoning cannot be sustained. If,

however, the ultimate conclusion that the disputed amount should not

be recovered from the respondent/complainant is viewed

independently through the prism of paragraph 12, namely, that the

appellant/opposite party Bank has not affirmatively discharged the

burden of establishing customer liability, the conclusion cannot be

rejected merely because Bank-side deficiency has not been

established. The two propositions are legally distinct. The award of

compensation stands on a still different footing. A finding that the

appellant/opposite party Bank has failed to establish customer liability

does not, without more, establish a compensable deficiency in service.

Compensation for mental agony/loss requires a legally sustainable

finding of deficiency or other actionable wrong and a rational nexus

between such wrong and the injury for which compensation is

awarded. The disputed transaction amount and compensation for

mental agony/loss are therefore conceptually distinct and cannot be

treated as interchangeable heads of relief. Accordingly, the award

of Rs.2 lakh towards mental agony/loss cannot be sustained
40
merely as a mathematical consequence of the disputed

transactions.
The age of the respondent/complainant may be a relevant

circumstance in considering the manner in which recovery measures

were undertaken, particularly in the context of the regulatory

safeguards governing recovery practices; but age, by itself, neither

determines the substantive liability for the disputed transactions nor

constitutes independent proof of compensable mental agony. The

question remains whether the appellant/opposite party Bank's

conduct, assessed against the applicable regulatory obligations and the

circumstances of the case, amounted to an actionable deficiency. The

controversy must therefore be resolved without conflating the two

distinct propositions which have run through the proceedings. The

failure to establish Bank-side deficiency is not proof of

customer liability; and the failure to establish customer liability

is not, by itself, proof of Bank-side deficiency. The governing

framework requires each question to be answered upon its own

evidentiary foundation. In that view of the matter, the reasoning of

the District Commission requires interference to the extent that it

treats the appellant/opposite party Bank's internal finding of

fraudulent transactions as an admission of Bank liability and, on that
41
basis alone, treats the subsequent demand notice as negligence and

deficiency. The reason is that inference does not follow or flow from

the evidence; at the same time, the appellant/opposite party Bank

cannot obtain an affirmative finding of customer liability merely by

relying upon the absence of proof of Bank deficiency. The burden

imposed by paragraph 12 of the RBI Circular DBR.No.Leg.BC.78/

09.07.005/2017-18 dated 6th July 2017 remains an independent and

substantive burden, and the material presently available does not

discharge it merely through proof of successful OTP authentication,

continued possession of the physical card and absence of detected

alteration in registered contact particulars.
Consequently, the issue framed for determination must,

therefore, be answered in its two limbs and not by allowing one to

swallow the other. The material on record is insufficient to fasten

the loss occasioned by the disputed transactions upon the

appellant/opposite party Bank as a consequence of fraud,

negligence or deficiency attributable to it; but, the same

material is also insufficient, without further affirmative

evidence, to establish the respondent/complainant's liability

for those transactions in the manner required by the governing

regulatory framework. The subsequent allegation of mobile
42
compromise does not establish third-party breach; equally, its failure

does not establish customer authorisation. The appellant/opposite

party Bank's investigation negatives demonstrated Bank-side

deficiency; it does not, without more, establish the respondent/

complainant as the person legally responsible for the disputed

transactions. The consequential treatment of the disputed amount

must accordingly proceed upon that distinction. The Bank's internal

characterisation of the transactions as fraudulent cannot, by

itself, sustain a finding of Bank liability; but the absence of

such liability cannot, by itself, convert the disputed amount

into an established customer default. Any recovery or default

action concerning the disputed amount must therefore conform to the

applicable regulatory framework governing disputed credit-card

transactions and cannot rest merely upon an assumption that the

failure of the respondent/complainant's alternative explanation has

discharged the Bank's independent burden of proving customer

liability.
12. In the result, the Appeal is allowed in part and

the order of the District Consumer Disputes Redressal

Commission, Chennai (South) passed in C.C. No.273 of 2023
43
dated 28.10.2025 is modified to the effect that the sum of

Rs.2,00,000/- awarded towards mental agony is set aside.

Except the above modification, in all other aspects the order of

the District Commission is confirmed. However, there is no

order as to costs in this appeal.
